claims.source: Measured on PySpark 4.0.4, local[2], in this repository.

claims.claim: Built-ins return NULL for NULL input; a Python UDF calling a string method on None raises PythonException.
claims.source: Run on PySpark 4.0.4 in this repository.

concept_html:
A Python UDF runs your Python function once per row. Spark must send each value from the JVM to a Python worker process, run the function, and send the result back. The physical plan shows this as a BatchEvalPython step.

A built-in function from pyspark.sql.functions runs inside the JVM, in Spark's generated code, with no round trip.

Measured on 2 million strings (PySpark 4.0.4, two local cores):

Approach Time
F.upper(col) 0.30 s
pandas UDF (ArrowEvalPython) 1.16 s
Python UDF (BatchEvalPython) 1.82 s

The Python UDF was six times slower, and the gap grows with cluster size and data volume.

Speed is one reason. There are three more:

  • Nulls. Built-ins return NULL for NULL input. A UDF receives None and must handle it. lambda s: s.strip() fails the whole job with a PythonException on the first NULL.
  • Optimisation. The optimiser cannot see inside a UDF, so it cannot push a filter on the UDF's output into the file scan.
  • Readability. F.when(...).when(...) states a rule in one expression a reviewer can check.

Most UDFs in pipelines replace functions that already exist: F.upper, F.trim, F.regexp_replace, F.regexp_extract, F.split, F.to_date, F.coalesce, F.when, F.concat_ws, F.lpad. Search the functions reference before you write one.

When no built-in fits, prefer a pandas UDF: it moves data in Arrow batches and runs vectorised pandas code. Use a row-by-row Python UDF only as the last resort, and handle None first.

lines: from pyspark.sql import Column
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
def clean_postcode(col: Column) -> Column:
"""Remove whitespace and upper-case. NULL stays NULL."""
return F.upper(F.regexp_replace(col, r"\s+", ""))
def age_band(age: Column) -> Column:
"""16-34, 35-54 or 55+. NULL age gives NULL."""
return (
F.when(age < 35, "16-34")
.when(age < 55, "35-54")
.when(age.isNotNull(), "55+")
)
silver = bronze.withColumns({
"postcode": clean_postcode(F.col("postcode")),
"age_group": age_band(F.col("age")),
})

notes.html: A function that builds a Column expression. Reusable and testable, with no UDF.
Built-ins pass NULL through as NULL.
Explicit: a NULL age stays NULL instead of falling into 55+.

example.takeaway_html: The strong version runs in the JVM, survives NULLs and reads as a rule. Functions that return Column expressions give you the reuse that UDFs promised.

lines: from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
@udf("string")
def clean_postcode(s):
return s.replace(" ", "").upper()
@udf("string")
def age_band(age):
if age < 35:
return "16-34"
if age < 55:
return "35-54"
return "55+"
silver = bronze.withColumn("postcode", clean_postcode("postcode")).withColumn("age_group", age_band("age"))

notes.html: Crashes on NULL: None has no replace method.
In Python, comparing None with 35 raises TypeError, so a NULL age crashes the job too.
Two round trips to Python per row, invisible to the optimiser.

wrong_answers.feedback: A Python UDF moves every value to a Python process and back. It measured about six times slower than a built-in.
A pandas UDF beats a Python UDF because it uses Arrow batches, but it still leaves the JVM. A built-in wins.
collect() pulls 50 million values onto one machine. It is the slowest option and can crash the driver.
Right choice, wrong reason. Built-ins run on the executors, like everything else. They win by staying in the JVM.

title: Built-in functions over Python UDFs
why_html:
A silver job cleans postcodes with a Python UDF: lambda s: s.replace(" ", "").upper(). It runs for months on deliveries where every postcode is present. Then a supplier sends a wave with 40 blank postcodes, which arrive as NULL. The first NULL raises AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'replace' inside a Python worker, and the whole silver job fails at 02:00.

F.upper(F.regexp_replace("postcode", r"\s+", "")) returns NULL for NULL, runs faster, and would never have failed.
